papers.title: Reimplementation of clickstream event sequence analysis model TRACE
papers.institution_note: HSLU logo on the cover; the CV places this work at the Applied Artificial Intelligence (AAI) Lab, HSLU
papers.abstract: On e-commerce websites, users often follow complex navigation paths while searching for products and ultimately completing a purchase. These navigation patterns generate clickstream data that captures detailed information about user interactions over time and across sessions. Such data can be leveraged to enhance personalization and improve recommendation systems by more effectively modeling user behavior and intent. This research presents a re-implementation and investigation of the TRACE architecture, a novel transformer-based approach designed to generate rich user embeddings from multi-session clickstream data for real-world recommendation applications. The study evaluates the effectiveness of TRACE in modeling complex user navigation patterns using alternative large-scale e-commerce datasets, due to the unavailability of the original dataset used in the TRACE paper.

original_paper.title: TRACE: Transformer-based user Representations from Attributed Clickstream Event sequences

description_points.text: Re-implements the TRACE architecture in PyTorch and evaluates it on alternative public e-commerce datasets, because the dataset used in the original TRACE paper is not publicly available.
TRACE uses a multi-task learning framework in which a shared Transformer encoder learns user representations by predicting several future engagement signals from clickstream event sequences.
Three public datasets were assessed (OTTO, Synerise RecSys Challenge 2025, RetailRocket); OTTO was used as the primary dataset for training and evaluation.
The model is compared against a single-task cohort (one TRACE model per task) and a multi-task Bi-LSTM baseline.

datasets.name: OTTO RecSys dataset
datasets.role: Primary dataset for training and evaluation

datasets.name: Synerise RecSys Challenge 2025 dataset
datasets.role: Assessed during dataset selection; viable but with fewer sessions than OTTO

datasets.name: RetailRocket recommender system dataset
datasets.role: Assessed and rejected: a 15-event minimum per session removed about 99.59% of sessions

method.architecture: Transformer encoder with multi-task output heads producing a shared user representation

tasks.definition: The user adds products to the cart at least two times during a session
The user views the same article (AID) at least four times within a session
The user purchases a product during the session

method.loss: Class-weighted binary cross-entropy (PyTorch BCEWithLogitsLoss with per-task positive-class weights)
method.data_preparation: Sessions with fewer than 32 events removed (1,621,909 of 3,164,777 sessions retained); each session split into input and target at a random point between 70% and 80% of its length

results.description: Average over the ATC, SAT and MAP tasks on the OTTO dataset (report Table 2)
findings: TRACE outperforms the multi-task Bi-LSTM baseline on all five metrics.
TRACE and the single-task cohort tie on AUROC (0.787); TRACE is slightly higher on AUPRC (0.696 vs 0.694), while the single-task cohort is slightly higher on binary F1, macro F1 and accuracy.
limitations: Evaluated on OTTO because the original TRACE dataset is not publicly available, so the numbers are not directly comparable with the original paper.
TRACE shows lower negative-class performance (higher false-positive rates) than both baselines; the report attributes this to the 70-80% input/target split and the class-weighting strategy.

repository.readme_title: Breast Cancer Survival Analysis — Classical vs. Deep Survival Models
repository.description: Application of Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning methods to the analysis of genomic and transcriptomic data in cancer

research_question.text: When we try to predict how long a breast-cancer patient will survive from their tumour's gene expression, do modern deep survival networks actually beat a well-regularised classical Cox model — or do they just look more impressive?

data.dataset: TCGA breast cancer RNA-seq (RSEM) expression and clinical data from cBioPortal, study brca_tcga_pub2015 (Breast Invasive Carcinoma, TCGA, Cell 2015)
data.survival_endpoint: Overall survival, administratively censored at 60 months

method.feature_selection: Low-expression filter (genes with more than 80% zero values removed), then limma differential expression and univariate Cox screening, fitted on the training split only
method.validation: Fixed patient split shared by all models (splits.json); hyperparameters chosen without the test set (k-fold cross-validation for Cox and Random Survival Forest models, validation set and grid search for DeepSurv and Cox-nnet); fixed random seed 42
method.evaluation: Harrell's concordance index (C-index) on held-out test patients; Kaplan–Meier curves and log-rank test on median-split high- and low-risk groups
method.interpretability: SHAP attributions with 50 bootstrap resamples for DeepSurv and Cox-nnet; gene-set enrichment against GO, KEGG and Reactome with GSEApy; STRING protein-protein interaction cross-check; Random Survival Forest minimal-depth interaction analysis

results.description: Results as reported in the thesis abstract (author decision NR-02)
findings: DeepSurv achieved the best discriminative performance (C-index of approximately 0.82).
DeepSurv was the only model to produce a statistically significant risk stratification, outperforming both the linear Cox models and the Random Survival Forest.
DeepSurv and Cox-nnet shared 257 prognostic genes in the bootstrap SHAP consensus.
limitations: The test set has about one hundred patients and no confidence interval is reported.
The neural networks' loss curves show overfitting.
There is no external validation cohort.
results.superseded_note: Per the author's decision, the per-model table from thesis Table 2 (page 27) and the repository README was removed. Those two sources still report different values (Cox-nnet highest with C-index 0.8750; DeepSurv 0.8032), so the hosted thesis PDF and the public README do not match the figures above.

Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

implementations.implementation: PyTorch LSTM encoder-decoder baseline (weights initialized uniformly between -0.08 and 0.08, following the Seq2Seq paper) and a bidirectional-GRU encoder with additive (Bahdanau) attention, compared with BLEU and ROUGE.
implementations.dataset: Synthetic dataset of 10,000 generated examples (create_dataset.py) that map natural-language reminders to structured task lists; the folder README says a synthetic dataset was used because no GPU was available.

verification.notes: The code (models/seq2seq_baseline.py, models/seq2seq_attention.py) implements the core model of each paper. Results come from a synthetic dataset rather than the papers' machine-translation benchmarks, so they are not comparable with published numbers.

implementations.name: Attention Is All You Need
implementations.implementation: Decoder-only, GPT-style Transformer language model (about 11 million parameters) with token and positional embeddings, causal masked multi-head self-attention, feed-forward layers, layer normalization and residual connections, trained for next-token prediction on a dataset of William Shakespeare's works on an NVIDIA L4 GPU, following Andrej Karpathy's 'Let's build GPT: from scratch' tutorial.

verification.notes: The code (gpt.py) implements the paper's scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, but not its encoder-decoder architecture; the folder README states the model is decoder-only 'instead of the traditional encoder-decoder structure'.

implementations.display_note: Describe as a decoder-only, GPT-style language model built on the paper's attention mechanism, not as a reproduction of the paper's encoder-decoder model.

architecture_figure.alt: Decoder-only Transformer diagram: input and output embeddings with positional encoding feed N stacked blocks of masked multi-head attention and feed-forward layers with add and norm, followed by a linear layer and softmax over output probabilities.
architecture_figure.caption: Decoder-only Transformer architecture used for the GPT-style model.
architecture_figure.credit: Adapted from Figure 1 of Vaswani et al. (2017), "Attention Is All You Need", arXiv:1706.03762.

implementations.name: Predicting Issue Types with seBERT
implementations.implementation: Fine-tunes a locally stored seBERT checkpoint (24-layer BERT encoder, hidden size 1024) with two binary heads, worth_automating and enough_information, on github-labels-annotated.csv using the Hugging Face Trainer.

verification.notes: The labels predicted (worth_automating, enough_information) are not the issue types named in the paper's title. The code imports modules that are not in the repository (src.classic_ml.*), and the evaluation cell scores the model on the full dataset, including training rows, so the printed metrics are not held-out results. No folder README.

implementations.display_note: Describe as fine-tuning the seBERT model from the paper for a different task (two binary labels: worth_automating and enough_information). Do not show the notebook's metrics; they were computed on data that includes the training set.

implementations.name: An Image Is Worth 16×16 Words

original_papers.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
original_papers.note: The main README links this arXiv ID; the folder README's arXiv link has a truncated ID and is not used.

implementations.implementation: Encoder-only Vision Transformer in PyTorch: 16x16 patch embedding (224x224 images into 196 patches), learnable [CLS] token and position embeddings, pre-norm encoder blocks with multi-head self-attention and a GELU MLP; 12 layers, hidden size 384, MLP size 1536, 6 attention heads, about 21.5 million parameters; trained on an NVIDIA L4 GPU.
implementations.dataset: Trained from scratch on Imagenette2 (10 classes), then partially fine-tuned (last two Transformer blocks, final layer normalization and a new head; 3.75M of 21.5M parameters trainable) on a 525-class bird species dataset.

reported_results.metric: Test accuracy on Imagenette2 (100 test images)
Validation accuracy after partial fine-tuning on 525 bird species

verification.notes: The code (model/ViT.py) implements the ViT method: patch embedding, [CLS] token, position embeddings and a Transformer encoder. It is trained at small scale from scratch, so accuracy is not comparable with the paper's results.

implementations.status_source: author decision 2026-10-18 (direct): the ViT reimplementation is finished. The Paper-Reimplementations README still says 'In Progress'.

architecture_figure.alt: Vision Transformer overview: an image is split into fixed-size patches, each patch is linearly projected and combined with a position embedding plus an extra learnable class embedding, passed through a Transformer encoder, and classified by an MLP head.

architecture_figure.credit: Figure 1 of Dosovitskiy et al. (2020), "An Image is Worth 16x16 Words", arXiv:2010.11929 (the repository README marks it as taken from the original paper).

needs_review.issue: The thesis abstract (English and Spanish, page iii) says DeepSurv had the best C-index (about 0.82) and was the only model with a statistically significant risk stratification. The thesis Results chapter (Table 2, page 27) and the repository README report Cox-nnet best (C-index 0.8750), DeepSurv 0.8032, and significant log-rank tests for every model except the Random Survival Forest (p = 0.1669). data.json uses the Table 2 and README values and omits the abstract.
needs_review.action: Confirm which results are correct.
needs_review.decision: DeepSurv is correct, matching the thesis abstract: best model, C-index approximately 0.82, and the only statistically significant risk stratification. The abstract's figures are used and the Table 2/README per-model table was removed. The hosted thesis PDF (Table 2) and the public README still show Cox-nnet 0.8750 as the best model.

needs_review.issue: The code fine-tunes a local seBERT checkpoint to predict 'worth_automating' and 'enough_information', not the issue types named in the paper. The notebook output also shows a local path 'Practicas_Manuel\T3.8.4'. data.json sets list_on_site = false.

needs_review.decision: seBERT (#03) stays public and is listed. Its description follows the code (fine-tuning seBERT for two binary labels). Data collector note: the notebook's metrics are excluded because they were computed on data that includes the training set.
